title: Joining Louis Armstrong's band: personnel and his steady playing
summary: After the Mallory band Wilson plays with Armstrong alongside Budd and Keg Johnson, admiring how Armstrong never complained and kept playing no matter the band.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: Well, when did you join Terry ... that's another story, I guess, huh?

Another story, right. That was after I left Chicago and went to New York. But at any rate, I was in Chicago and I was playing with the Milt Senior band at the Gold Coast Club and then after that folded, there was

Eddie Mallory's band, as we spoke of earlier -- the Villa enice, and I worked with Buddand Keg Johnson in that band, and then after Eddie Mallory band, I joined Louis Armstrong's band. Louis Armstrong was based in Chicago in those days, and Budd and Keg and I --

Silver Brown, yeah. He was the musical director for Louis, and the first trumpet player, and we had Mike McKendrick on banjo, and Yank Porter was our drummer. Louis had gotten a hold of Yank Porter, a drummer from New York. Then the Walton Brothers -- one was playing bass and the other played saxophone.

And Budd Johnson on tenor sax and Keg Johnson on trombone. Well, that was really something for me to play with Louis Armstrong, because I had idolized this man so much, and he was as influential in developing my music as the piano players that I used to listen to, I would say.

And another thing I learned about Armstrong -- on the road, playing night after night, Armstrong would go straight ahead in this sense -- no matter how bad the man played or anything, Armstrong went right straight ahead, he was always right and he was not at the mercy of the drummer or the saxophones, the rest of the band, and he never complained to any musician.
The band could be terrible, and he just went right straight ahead and played in that world of his own and was never at the mercy of the band.
And you can see that now --you hear his records now and you can hear that.

Yeah. And so many great artists are at the mercy of the piano player or at the mercy of the drummer, I know a great singer was supposed to have stopped her show once in Birdland and cursed the piano player right over the microphone, as to what the devil are you playing, and using very strong language, you know? But Armstrong in public, you never knew. And the band could be messing up behind him ...

And he didn't want anybody to tell you, If you were new in the band, he would prefer that you join without having the distraction of people telling you, a B-minor 7 or a C7--7 because I know in later years when I joined his band, somebody would tell me something and he would just turn around and throw the chord to you. Da, da, da.
And he said to me, 'Glad you're here, you're sounding good!'
